results.title: Nvidia’s H100 GPU prices rebound after years of decline, signalling market volatility | Noah Intelligence
highlights:
For much of the past three years, the cost of renting Nvidia’s H100 graphics processors looked as if it were obeying a quieter version of Moore’s Law: relentless, and for buyers of compute, welcome. Silicon Data’s pricing history shows on-demand H100 rates falling from more than $7 an hour in 2023 to roughly $2 by mid-2025, while other industry trackers put the overall drop at as much as 75% from the chip’s early peak. That slide has made AI inference and training far cheaper than many investors expected when shortages were at their worst.

...

Yet the market has not moved in a straight line. Data cited by SemiAnalysis and other pricing trackers show that one-year H100 contract rates began to rebound late in 2025, rising about 40% from an October low by March 2026. December 2025 also saw a roughly 10% monthly jump in on-demand rates. The increase did not erase the longer decline, but it did interrupt the idea that AI compute costs only move one way.

The latest pricing guides suggest the market remains volatile rather than structurally tight. IntuitionLabs puts current on-demand H100 rentals across major clouds at roughly $1.49 to $6.98 an hour, while GPUCloudList says rates had eased to around $2.00 to $4.15 by March 2026. Presenc AI similarly describes the market as having moved from acute scarcity in 2023 to a more balanced supply picture by 2026, with spot pricing sometimes even lower.

A2 instances (NVIDIA A100) serve training and inference workloads across two variants: a2-highgpu with A100 40 GB GPUs and a2-megagpu with A100 80 GB GPUs. On-demand pricing for A100 instances is approximately 3.60to 3.60 t o 3.70 per GPU-hour, with committed use discounts and spot pricing reducing effective rates substantially. A2 instances remain a strong option for workloads that do not require H100-class performance.

G2 instances (NVIDIA L4) target inference-optimized and graphics workloads. The g2-standard family provides L4 GPUs at approximately $0.70 per GPU-hour on-demand in us-central1. L4 instances are cost-efficient for model serving, video processing, and lighter AI workloads that do not require the compute power of H100 or A100 GPUs.

results.title: Amazon EC2 GPU Alternatives: 5 Cloud Providers Compared | Markaicode
highlights:
What this is not: a lab benchmark. GPU marketplace pricing changes hourly and varies by host/region, so a single-run throughput number would be stale by the time you read it. Vendor-published rates are marked and dated below; anything unverifiable is described qualitatively instead.

...

1. Pricing structure. EC2 GPU on-demand rates bill per instance-hour with per-second granularity, but effective cost is driven by idle time between jobs and by whether you've committed to Reserved Instances or Savings Plans — commitments that don't fit unpredictable GPU demand. AWS cut P5/P4d on-demand pricing by up to 45% and 33% respectively in mid-2025, which narrowed but didn't close this gap.
2. GPU availability during demand spikes. Popular types (P5, P4d) can have limited on-demand capacity in specific regions at peak demand; AWS has since expanded at-scale on-demand capacity for P4d/P5 in additional regions in direct response.
3. Provisioning and cold-start overhead. Standing up a new EC2 GPU instance (AMI, user data scripts, security group and IAM wiring) takes longer than deploying on a GPU-specialist platform, and autoscaling GPU fleets on EC2 needs more custom tooling than the built-in autoscalers most specialist clouds ship with.

...

### RunPod — Serverless GPU Endpoints Without EC2's Provisioning Overhead

Who it's for: teams running containerized inference (vLLM, TGI, custom FastAPI servers) who want autoscaling without building their own CloudWatch-driven scaler.

Hard limits: serverless workers drop SSH access (Pods keep it); public endpoints run through RunPod's proxy domain by default. Per RunPod's July 27, 2026 pricing page, on-demand Secure Cloud runs $1.39/hr for an A100 PCIe 80GB and $2.89/hr for an H100 PCIe, with Serverless A100 inference priced separately at $2.72/hr; Community Cloud is typically cheaper but floats with third-party capacity and isn't on a fixed card.

...

### Vast.ai — Marketplace Pricing, Marketplace Risk

Who it's for: fault-tolerant batch jobs (offline inference, data preprocessing, non-critical fine-tuning) that can checkpoint and resume.

Hard limits: a peer-to-peer marketplace — you're renting from individual hosts. Vast.ai's own product page advertises on-demand rates "as little as $0.90/hour" for an H100, but that's a floor set by whichever host is competing for your business that hour, not a guaranteed rate. Storage and bandwidth bill separately and keep running on stopped instances until deleted.

...

### Lambda — Flat-Rate Dedicated GPUs, No Spot Surprises

Who it's for: long training or fine-tuning jobs that need a GPU that won't be reclaimed mid-run, without managing spot-interruption logic.

Hard limits: per Lambda's own pricing page, on-demand self-serve tops out at H100 SXM ($3.99/hr) and B200 SXM6 ($6.69/hr); A100 80GB SXM runs $2.79/hr. Availability is first-come, self-serve — no guarantee a given model is available in your region the moment you need it.

...

Hard limits: per DigitalOcean's official Paperspace pricing docs, on-demand rates run from about $0.45/hr for entry GPUs up to $3.18/hr for an A100-80G and $5.95/hr for H100 — H100 availability is limited versus specialist GPU clouds, and multi-GPU H100 nodes need a reserved contract, not self-serve on-demand.

results.title: Best GPU Cloud for AI 2026: RunPod vs Vast.ai vs Lambda Labs Compared
highlights:
### RunPod — Best Overall for AI Inference

RunPod has quietly become the go-to GPU cloud for indie AI developers. Its serverless GPU offering lets you deploy model endpoints with autoscaling from zero — you only pay when inference runs. The key innovation is that RunPod handles cold starts (loading models onto GPUs) in 5-10 seconds, making serverless actually viable for interactive AI applications.

Pricing starts at $0.12/hr for RTX 4090 (spot) and $0.59/hr for A100 80GB (on-demand). The serverless tier charges per second of GPU time plus a small memory fee — a typical Llama 70B inference request costs about $0.001-0.003.

⚠️ Limitation: RunPod’s spot instances can be interrupted. For latency-sensitive applications, you’ll want the on-demand tier which costs 2-3x more.

### Vast.ai — Cheapest, but Rough Around the Edges

Vast.ai operates a marketplace where GPU owners (from individuals with desktop GPUs to small datacenters) rent out their hardware. This means prices can be shockingly low: $0.08-0.15/hr for RTX 4090 and $0.35-0.60/hr for A100. During off-peak hours, you can find RTX 3090s for under $0.05/hr.

The catch: hardware quality varies. A “4090” from one provider might deliver 80% of the performance of another’s because of thermal throttling, driver versions, or bandwidth limits. The CLI and API are functional but not polished. Customer support is community-driven via Discord.

⚠️ Limitation: No serverless/autoscaling — you rent whole instances. For batch processing or training, Vast.ai is excellent. For production inference with variable load, RunPod handles it better.

### Lambda Labs — Premium, Predictable, Priced Accordingly

Lambda Labs is the “AWS of GPU clouds” — premium hardware, guaranteed availability, excellent support, and pricing that reflects it. RTX 4090 on-demand starts at $0.35/hr and A100 80GB at $1.10/hr. You get consistent performance, no spot interruptions, and a polished API.

Lambda also offers GPU instances with high-speed InfiniBand interconnects, which matter if you’re doing multi-node training. For simple inference, you’re paying for reliability you might not need.

⚠️ Limitation: Pricing is 2-3x RunPod’s spot rates. For early-stage projects, the premium is hard to justify.

results.title: Moore's Law, AI Compute Costs and Semiconductor Bounce
highlights:
In December 2025, on-demand H100 rentals jumped roughly 10% in a single month, and by March 2026 one-year contract rates had climbed about 40% from their October 2025 low, according to pricing data from Silicon Data and SemiAnalysis. The bounce interrupted a three-year price collapse and reset how investors should read Moore’s Law, AI compute costs, and the semiconductor cycle.

### Key facts at a glance

- H100 on-demand rates fell roughly 64% to 75% from their 2023 peak of $8 to $12 per GPU-hour to a 2026 range of $1.49 to $6.98 across major clouds, per IntuitionLabs.
- One-year H100 contract rates rose from about $1.70 per hour in October 2025 to about $2.35 by March 2026, a roughly 40% bounce, per SemiAnalysis.
- Introl pegged the December 2025 on-demand cut at 64% from the 2023 highs before the spike landed.
- Crypto Briefing reported Nvidia (NVDA) lifting reference rental rates around 20% into 2026.

...

The long-run direction is down. Silicon Data’s 2023-to-2025 dataset shows the on-demand H100 falling from a 2023 peak above $8 per hour to roughly $2 by mid-2025, a curve much closer to Moore’s Law than the AI bears expected.

Eugene Cheah at Latent Space called the floor in 2024 by counting newly built colocation capacity, and Spheron now lists H100 SXM from $1.03 per hour.

results.title: Daily Investment Brief — June 14, 2026 | Signwl
highlights:
The GPU compute market is undergoing a structural bifurcation between training and inference tiers that is more advanced than spot prices alone suggest. AWS Inferentia spot in Virginia has collapsed 90%+ from its January peak of $0.125/hr to a current $0.013/hr — the pricing signature of a commercially wound-down product — while Trainium spot in Ohio has undergone a deliberate step-change activation since late January, with prices rising from near-zero to a managed $0.178/hr range. This ASIC rotation is the clearest signal in the dataset. Overlaid on this, the Montreal H100 spot market's 90-day history reveals a full downward convergence cycle (from $7.46/hr in January to a $1.9/hr trough in mid-May, now re-inflating to $4.98/hr with a 197% spread) — a cautionary case study in how dangerous cross-sectional spot snapshots can be for procurement decisions. The dominant macro theme is power: GPU supply geography is visibly reorganizing around energy availability (GCP L4 emerging in Nevada and Iowa at near-zero spot prices), and operators who have secured power supply independence — Nebius's $2.6B, 10-year Bloom Energy deal for its Missouri gigawatt campus — are building a structural moat that grid-dependent competitors have not matched.

...

1. Inferentia SPOT Virginia collapsed from $0.125/hr in early January 2026 to a trough of $0.003/hr by mid-February — a 97% collapse — before stabilizing in a low-volatility band currently at $0.013/hr (live pricing data, June 14, 2026). This is a scrap-rate clearing pattern, not normal market fluctuation.
2. Inferentia on-demand pricing has remained absolutely frozen across all US regions and Hong Kong for 30+ days — zero movement — confirming AWS has stopped active commercial management of the platform. Spot and OD are completely decoupled.
3. Trainium SPOT Ohio underwent a step-change activation around January 25, 2026: prices jumped from near-zero (~$0.004/hr) to $0.255/hr and peaked at $0.490/hr on February 21 before settling into a dynamically managed $0.10–0.178/hr range (live pricing history, June 14, 2026). This is active fleet management, not passive availability.
4. Trainium SPOT in Melbourne simultaneously collapsed -82.4% over 30 days — consistent with AWS concentrating Trainium capacity in US home regions while letting APAC spot drain, a classic fleet rationalization move.
5. Amazon Q1 2026 earnings disclosure confirmed: "Trainium 2 and Inferentia 3 chips deployed to shift workloads away from Nvidia H100/H200 infrastructure" (abhs.in, June 13, 2026) — direct management confirmation of the architectural pivot.
6. CATALOG_SURVIVAL data shows Inferentia has been active in AWS catalog for 6.5 years — consistent with an end-of-life product whose catalog presence lags its commercial relevance.
7. Broadcom and Marvell control approximately 95% of custom ASIC co-design, with ASICs projected to capture 27.8% of AI server compute market share in 2026, growing 44.6% YoY (AOL, June 14, 2026) — the structural tailwind for Trainium2 demand is real.
8. Qualifying evidence: Trainium on-demand pricing is also frozen at $0.94/hr across Ohio, Oregon, and Virginia with zero 30-day delta. Until AWS cuts Inferentia on-demand pricing by 20–30% (the classic deprecation announcement move), the transition remains visible in spot but officially unacknowledged — reducing certainty on the timeline.
